raw_findings.message: The handler reads the full client-supplied Content-Length without a size limit, so a large or incomplete body can exhaust memory or tie up a request thread.
Account lists and the other account and statement GET routes do not check the caller's identity, exposing every owner's balances and statements.
Converting JSON amounts with int() silently truncates fractional values such as 1.9 to 1 instead of rejecting non-integer cents.
Transfer and close requests never verify that X-Owner owns the targeted account, so any caller can debit or close another owner's account.
The account label is interpolated into HTML without escaping, so a label containing script markup executes when its statement is viewed.
Negative offsets or limits are passed directly to Python slicing, allowing requests to return unintended tail entries or omit entries.
Only the upper deposit limit is enforced, so a negative initial_cents value creates an account with a negative balance.
Request fields are copied onto the account without an allowlist, letting a caller set protected fields such as balance_cents or id and bypass the deposit cap or overwrite an existing account.
The funds check excludes the 25-cent fee, so a transfer equal to the source balance is accepted and leaves that account overdrawn.
Negative amounts pass the funds check and reverse the transfer direction, so a caller can increase the source balance while taking funds from the destination.
Concurrent transfers can read the same source balance before either writes it, causing lost debits and inconsistent ledger balances.
Transfers do not check the destination's closed flag, so funds can be credited to an account after it has been closed.

The house account is accepted as a transfer source, and when it is the source the following fee assignment overwrites its debit, allowing the destination to receive funds without the house paying them.
The source and house balances are changed before the destination is validated, so transferring to an unknown account returns an error after partially applying the transfer.
Closing an already-closed account is not rejected, so every repeat appends another close entry to its statement.

fixed_raw_findings.message: Account creation does not bind the requested owner to the caller's X-Owner identity, so a caller authenticated as one owner can create accounts assigned to another owner.
Ownership is established solely by comparing the account owner to the client-supplied X-Owner header, so any API caller who supplies a victim's owner value can read or mutate that victim's accounts.
int() silently truncates fractional JSON amounts, so a request for a transfer of 1.9 cents is executed as a transfer of 1 cent rather than being rejected.
The upper cap does not reject negative initial_cents, allowing an account to be created with a negative balance despite the API describing this value as an initial deposit.
A missing owner is stored as an empty string, but app.py's _owned rejects accounts with empty owners, leaving the created account and its balance inaccessible.

raw_findings.message: The accounts list returns every owner's balances and account details without checking X-Owner, so any caller can read all accounts.
Transfers do not verify that X-Owner owns the source account, so any caller who knows an account ID can debit it.
The close endpoint does not verify that X-Owner owns the requested account, so any caller can close another owner's account.
The account label is interpolated into HTML without escaping, so a label containing script markup executes when the HTML statement is viewed.
Negative offset or limit values are passed directly to Python slicing, allowing requests such as offset=-2 to return entries from the end of the statement.
The initial deposit is capped only above, so a negative initial_cents value creates an account with a negative balance.
Account creation trusts the request body's owner instead of verifying it against X-Owner, allowing a caller to create accounts attributed to another owner.
Every request field is assigned directly to the Account, so a caller can overwrite fields such as id, balance_cents, or entries and even replace the house account.
Transfers never check the accounts' closed flags, so closed accounts can still send or receive funds.
The coverage check compares the source balance only with the transfer amount, so a transfer can be accepted even when the balance cannot cover the additional fee.
Negative amounts pass the coverage check and make a transfer increase the source balance while decreasing the destination balance.
Concurrent transfers can read the same balances before the journal sleep and then overwrite one another's balance updates, leaving balances inconsistent with accepted transfers.
The journal is written and the source and house balances are changed before the destination is validated, so transferring to an unknown account returns an error after destroying funds.
Closing an already-closed account succeeds and appends another close entry, so repeated requests corrupt its statement history.

raw_findings.message: Account listings and other account-reading routes do not check the caller's X-Owner, so any caller can view every owner's account details and balances.
The transfer route never verifies that X-Owner owns the source account, so any caller can debit arbitrary accounts, including the house account.
The close route does not verify that X-Owner owns the requested account, so any caller can close another owner's account.
The account label is interpolated into HTML without escaping, so a label containing script markup executes when a statement is viewed.
Negative offsets are passed directly to Python slicing, so a request such as offset=-2 returns entries from the end of the statement instead of rejecting the offset.
Only an upper bound is applied to the initial deposit, so a negative initial_cents value creates an account with a negative balance.
The account owner is taken from the request body without checking it against X-Owner, so a caller can create an account attributed to another owner.
Request fields are assigned directly to the account, allowing callers to bypass the deposit cap by setting balance_cents or replace an existing account by setting id.
Transfers do not check whether either account is closed, so a closed account can still send or receive funds.
The cover check verifies only the transfer amount and not the fee, so a balance equal to the amount can be driven 25 cents below zero.
The cover check accepts negative amounts, so a caller can transfer a negative value to increase the source balance and debit the destination.
Transfers read balances before a sleep and later overwrite them without synchronization, so concurrent transfers can lose balance updates.
The source and house balances are changed before the destination is validated, so transferring to an unknown account returns an error after changing ledger balances.
Transfer fees change the house balance without adding a corresponding house statement entry, so the ledger's statements omit those balance movements.
Closing an already-closed account is allowed and appends another close entry, so repeated requests produce duplicate closures in its statement.

fixed_raw_findings.message: The handler reads the entire client-supplied Content-Length without a size limit, so oversized or slow request bodies can exhaust memory or tie up server threads.
This iteration is not synchronized with account creation, so concurrent POST /accounts requests can change the dictionary during iteration and make GET /accounts fail with a 500 response.
Account creation accepts the body’s owner without checking it against the caller identity, so a request can create an account that appears in another owner's account list.
Authorization trusts the caller-supplied X-Owner value without authenticating it, so a caller can set it to another account's owner and read, close, or transfer from that account.
Account reads do not acquire the ledger lock, so a GET concurrent with a transfer or close can observe balances partway through the multi-account update.
The upper-only cap accepts negative initial_cents, allowing creation of accounts with negative balances and, when closed, reducing the house balance.
Closing an account credits the house balance but adds no corresponding credit entry to the house account, leaving its statement inconsistent with its balance and the closed account's entry.
